The role of implicit regularization.
While explicit regularizers like dropout and weight-decay
may not be essential for generalization, it is certainly the case that not all models that ﬁt the training
data well generalize well. Indeed, in neural networks, we almost always choose our model as the
output of running stochastic gradient descent. Appealing to linear models, we analyze how SGD
acts as an implicit regularizer. For linear models, SGD always converges to a solution with small
norm. Hence, the algorithm itself is implicitly regularizing the solution. Indeed, we show on small
data sets that even Gaussian kernel methods can generalize well with no regularization. Though this
doesn’t explain why certain architectures generalize better than other architectures, it does suggest
that more investigation is needed to understand exactly what the properties are inherited by models
that were trained using SGD.

With more expressive kernels, one could use Gaus-
sian processes to learn hidden representations in data.
Expressive kernels have been developed by combining
Gaussian processes in a type of Bayesian neural net-
work structure (Salakhutdinov & Hinton, 2008; Wilson
et al., 2012; Damianou & Lawrence, 2012). However,
these approaches, while promising, typically 1) are
designed to model speciﬁc types of structure (e.g.,
input-dependent correlations between diﬀerent tasks);
2) make use of component GPs with simple interpo-
lating kernels; 3) indirectly induce complicated ker-
nels that do not have a closed form and are diﬃcult
to interpret; and 4) require sophisticated approximate
inference techniques that are much more demanding
than that required by simple analytic kernels.

4. Experiments

We show how the SM kernel in Eq. (12) can be used
to discover patterns, extrapolate, and model negative
covariances. We contrast the SM kernel with pop-
ular kernels in, e.g., Rasmussen & Williams (2006)
and Abrahamsen (1997), which typically only provide
smooth interpolation. Although the SM kernel gen-
erally improves predictive likelihood over popular al-
ternatives, we focus on clearly visualizing the learned
kernels and spectral densities, examining patterns and
predictions, and discovering structure in the data. Our
objective is to elucidate the fundamental diﬀerences
between the proposed SM kernel and the alternatives.

marginalization over the unknown function can be per-
formed in closed form. Kernel hyperparameters are
trained using nonlinear conjugate gradients to opti-
mize the marginal likelihood p(y|θ, {xn}N
n=1) of the
data y given hyperparameters θ, as described in Sec-
tion 2, assuming a zero mean GP. A type of “auto-
matic relevance determination” (MacKay et al., 1994;
Tipping, 2004) takes place during training, minimizing
the eﬀect of extraneous components in the proposed
model, through the complexity penalty in the marginal
likelihood (Rasmussen & Williams, 2006). The com-
plexity penalty in the log marginal likelihood is a log
determinant which can be written as a sum of eigenval-
ues of a covariance matrix. Extraneous weights shrink
towards zero, since they will increase the eigenvalues
of this covariance matrix, without signiﬁcantly improv-
ing the model ﬁt. Moreover, the exponential terms in
the SM kernel of Eq. (12) have an annealing eﬀect on
the marginal likelihood, reducing multimodality in the
frequency parameters, making it easier to naively op-

timize the marginal likelihood without converging to
undesirable local optima. For a fully Bayesian treat-
ment, the spectral density could alternatively be inte-
grated out using Markov chain Monte Carlo (Murray
& Adams, 2010), rather than choosing a point esti-
mate. However, we wish to emphasize that the SM
kernel can be successfully used in the same way as
other popular kernels, without additional inference ef-
forts.

We compare with the popular squared exponential
(SE), Mat´ern (MA), rational quadratic (RQ), and pe-
riodic (PE) kernels. In each comparison, we attempt
to give these alternative kernels fair treatment: we
initialise hyperparameters at values that give high
marginal likelihoods and which are well suited to the
datasets, based on features we can already see in the
data. Conversely, we randomly initialise the param-
eters for the SM kernel. Training runtimes are on
the order of minutes for all tested kernels. In these
examples, comparing with multiple kernel learning
(MKL) (G¨onen & Alpaydın, 2011) has limited addi-
tional value. MKL is not typically intended for pat-
tern discovery, and often uses mixtures of SE kernels.
Mixtures of SE kernels correspond to scale-mixtures of
Gaussian spectral densities, and do not perform well
on these data, which are described by highly multi-
modal non-Gaussian spectral densities.

## Gaussian Process Kernels

The corpus contains one paper directly on this topic — **Andrew Gordon Wilson & Ryan Prescott Adams, "Gaussian Process Kernels for Pattern Discovery and Extrapolation"** (`1302.4245.pdf`, ICML 2013). Every other corpus hit for these words is incidental (e.g. "memory kernels," "Gaussian noise"); the one exception worth noting is flagged at the end. Here is a complete account drawn from that paper.

### The problem with standard kernels

In a Gaussian process (a Bayesian nonparametric distribution over functions), the kernel/covariance function determines everything about the learned functions — smoothness, periodicity, and how quickly the function varies (p. 3). The popular **squared exponential (SE) kernel**, `kSE(x,x′) = exp(−0.5‖x−x′‖²/ℓ²)`, produces infinitely differentiable functions but is "simply a smoothing device": the only structure it can learn from data is a single length-scale ℓ (p. 3). Other standard choices — Matérn (MA), rational quadratic (RQ), and periodic (PE) — likewise mostly provide smooth interpolation and require a human to inspect the data and hard-code the structure into the covariance (p. 4).

### The key idea: model the spectral density with a Gaussian mixture

The authors work in the frequency domain via **Bochner's theorem** (p. 3): any stationary kernel `k(τ)`, where `τ = x−x′`, is the Fourier dual of a spectral density `S(s)`, so the spectral density *entirely determines* the kernel. The SE kernel corresponds only to a single Gaussian spectral density centered at the origin — "a very small corner of the set of possible stationary kernels" (p. 3).

Their insight: because **mixtures of Gaussians are dense in the set of all distributions**, modeling the spectral density as a scale-location mixture of Gaussians (with non-zero means) lets you approximate *any* stationary covariance kernel to arbitrary precision, given enough components (p. 3).

### The spectral mixture (SM) kernel

Starting from a single Gaussian spectral component, the Fourier transform gives the closed form (Eq. 11, p. 3):

> `k(τ) = exp{−2π²τ²σ²} · cos(2πτµ)`

Generalizing to a mixture of Q Gaussians on RᴾΩ, with component weights `w_q`, means `µ_q`, and variances `v_q`, yields the **spectral mixture (SM) kernel** (Eq. 12, pp. 3–4):

> `k(τ) = Σ_{q=1}^{Q} w_q · Π_{p=1}^{P} exp{−2π²τ_p² v_q^(p)} · cos(2πτ_p µ_q^(p))`

The parameters are directly interpretable (p. 4): the weights `w_q` give each component's relative contribution, the inverse means `1/µ_q` are the component **periods**, and the inverse standard deviations `1/√v_q` are **length-scales**. It is a drop-in replacement for standard kernels, and — importantly — GP inference stays simple and analytic: assuming Gaussian noise, hyperparameters are trained by optimizing the marginal likelihood with nonlinear conjugate gradients, and an automatic-relevance-determination effect shrinks unneeded components toward zero (p. 4).

### Experimental results

The paper demonstrates that the SM kernel discovers structure and extrapolates where standard kernels fail:

- **Atmospheric CO₂ (Mauna Loa):** trained on the first 200 months, extrapolating ~25 years ahead — the standard tutorial example where a human normally hard-codes trend + seasonality (p. 4).
- **Negative-covariance AR(1) process:** the learned SM covariance accurately reconstructs the true covariance; its spectral density shows a sharp peak at frequency 0.5 (period 2), capturing the sign-flipping oscillation. Q=4 specified, only 3 components used after training (p. 7).
- **Sinc pattern** (sum of three sinc functions): from 700 training points, the SM kernel (Q=10, 7 used) reconstructs the held-out region x∈[−4.5, 4.5] "almost perfectly," with 95% of the posterior mass containing the true pattern, while SE, Matérn, RQ, and periodic kernels entirely miss it (pp. 7–8).
- **Airline passengers (1949–1961):** forecasting 48 months from the first 96, the SM kernel simultaneously interpolates and extrapolates complex structure. Its learned spectral density cleanly separates a low-frequency rising trend (~0.00148), a yearly 12-month cycle, and a ~3-month seasonal peak — where standard kernels are forced to choose between modeling short-term variation or the long-term trend (p. 8).

Predictive performance across all these is tabulated in the paper's Table 1 (referenced on pp. 7–8).

### Summary

The paper's contribution is the **spectral mixture (SM) kernel**: a closed-form, interpretable, stationary GP kernel built by modeling the spectral density as a Gaussian mixture. It can approximate any stationary covariance, reconstruct standard kernels (SE, Matérn, etc.) as special cases, and — unlike them — automatically *discover* periodic/multi-scale patterns and extrapolate them, all while keeping GP inference simple and analytic (abstract p. 1; pp. 3–4).

---

**One incidental cross-reference:** `1611.03530.pdf` ("Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization"), p. 3, notes that "even Gaussian kernel methods can generalize well with no regularization" — this is about generalization theory, not about GP kernel design, so it doesn't bear on the substance above.
